````
- path: README.md
  content: |
      # RuleForge
      
      **A local detection-rule workbench for enterprise SIEM rules.**
      
      Author a rule once, read it in eight dialects, test it against real log samples,
      and keep the history of how it changed.
      
      ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.10%2B-3776AB?logo=python&logoColor=white)
      ![Dependencies](https://img.shields.io/badge/dependencies-none-brightgreen)
      ![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-1345%20passing-brightgreen)
      ![Dialects](https://img.shields.io/badge/dialects-8-blue)
      ![Corpus](https://img.shields.io/badge/corpus-403%20rules-blue)
      
      ---
      
      ## Contents
      
      - [Why this exists](#why-this-exists)
      - [Features](#features)
      - [Quick start](#quick-start)
      - [The workbench](#the-workbench)
      - [Command line](#command-line)
      - [Supported dialects](#supported-dialects)
      - [Three verdicts](#three-verdicts)
      - [Refusals](#refusals)
      - [Design principles](#design-principles)
      - [Project structure](#project-structure)
      - [Testing](#testing)
      - [Known limitations](#known-limitations)
      - [Scope and security](#scope-and-security)
      - [Requirements](#requirements)
      - [Contributing](#contributing)
      - [License](#license)
      
      ---
      
      ## Why this exists
      
      Every design decision in RuleForge comes from a single failure mode:
      
      > **A rule that matches more than its author intended, while reporting success.**
      
      That is worse than a crash. A crash is loud, gets investigated, and gets fixed.
      A rule that silently widened from *"five failed logons from one account"* to
      *"any failed logon"* returns a green check mark and gets deployed — and nobody
      investigates a green result.
      
      RuleForge is built to make that outcome impossible. It does not approximate the
      hard parts of a conversion. When a rule cannot cross a dialect boundary without
      changing meaning, it refuses by name, states what would have gone wrong, and
      exits non-zero.
      
      It is a **workbench**, not a SIEM and not a deployment tool. It parses untrusted
      rule text, evaluates rules against untrusted samples, and never claims to know
      your data volume.
      
      ---
      
      ## Features
      
      | | |
      |---|---|
      | **Read a rule you did not write** | Paste a Sigma rule, a Splunk search, a KQL query, Wazuh XML, AQL, EQL, YARA-L or an FQL filter. It comes back as a structured rule with an outline that says, in prose, what the thing actually matches — including the parts that do not mean what they look like. |
      | **Convert between dialects** | Any supported dialect to any other. What *cannot* cross is reported rather than dropped. |
      | **Test against samples** | Paste events and get `matched`, `no_match` or `not_evaluated`, with a stage-by-stage trace of where rows were lost. |
      | **Propose a rule from logs** | Paste several samples of the same behaviour and it reports which fields are stable enough to be a detection, and which only looked stable. The output is labelled a hypothesis, because it is one. |
      | **Keep the history** | Every saved rule records its origin — `authored`, `imported` or `synthesized` — and its parent, so a rule's lineage stays readable. |
      | **Run headless** | The same engine from a shell, with refusals on stderr and the answer in the exit code. A detection engineer cannot put a browser in CI. |
      
      ---
      
      ## Quick start
      
      ```bash
      git clone https://github.com/EclipseManic/RuleForge.git
      cd RuleForge
      python run.py
      ```
      
      ```
        RuleForge -- Detection Rule Workbench
        http://127.0.0.1:8765/
      
        Eight dialects, one rule model, standard library only.
        Ctrl+C to stop.
      ```
      
      There is **no install step, no build step and no configuration.** `run.py` is
      the only entry point; it puts the repository on `sys.path` itself.
      
      Verify the checkout before you trust it:
      
      ```bash
      python run.py verify
      ```
      
      That runs the full test suite and then sweeps 403 real-shaped rules through all
      eight dialects.
      
      ---
      
      ## The workbench
      
      `python run.py` serves a single-page interface from the Python standard library
      at `http://127.0.0.1:8765/`, in two sections:
      
      **Home** — where you left off, recent history, and quick actions.
      
      **Studio** — the working surface, in six panes:
      
      | Pane | Purpose |
      |---|---|
      | **Workbench** | Build and edit a rule against the vendor-neutral model, with live rendering into a target dialect |
      | **Import & Explain** | Paste a rule in any supported language and read back a plain-language outline of what it matches |
      | **From Log** | Derive a candidate rule from log samples, with each field marked stable or volatile |
      | **Datasets** | Saved, hashed event samples used as replay evidence |
      | **Test Runs** | Immutable records of a rule version run against a dataset, with verdict and stage trace |
      | **History** | Every saved version, its origin, and its lineage |
      
      Options:
      
      ```bash
      python run.py serve --port 9000     # try a different port
      python run.py serve --no-browser    # do not open a browser
      python run.py serve --host 127.0.0.1
      ```
      
      If the preferred port is busy, `run.py` moves to the next free one and tells you
      which port it actually bound — it never prints a URL it is not serving.
      
      ---
      
      ## Command line
      
      `run.py` serves the workbench, runs the repository's own checks, and passes
      everything else straight through to the engine CLI. There is one parser to
      learn, not two that can disagree.
      
      ```bash
      python run.py dialects                            # list the eight dialects
      python run.py check     sigma    rule.yml         # parse, validate, report losses
      python run.py explain   sigma    rule.yml         # say what the rule matches
      python run.py convert   sigma sentinel rule.yml   # translate
      python run.py test      sigma    rule.yml events.jsonl
      python run.py propose   samples.jsonl --target sigma
      ```
      
      `-` reads from stdin, so the subcommands compose:
      
      ```bash
      python run.py convert sigma splunk rule.yml | python run.py check splunk -
      ```
      
      ### Exit codes
      
      | Code | Meaning |
      |---|---|
      | `0` | The work succeeded |
      | `1` | A rule was refused, or a conversion lost something |
      | `2` | The arguments were wrong |
      
      A **lossy conversion exits `1` even though it printed the text**, so a pipeline
      cannot deploy a widened rule without noticing.
      
      ---
      
      ## Supported dialects
      
      | Key | Vendor | Language | Reads | Writes | Carries metadata |
      |---|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|---|
      | `sentinel` | Microsoft Sentinel | KQL | yes | yes | as a `//` header |
      | `sigma` | Sigma | YAML | yes | yes | natively |
      | `splunk` | Splunk | SPL | yes | yes | no — see below |
      | `qradar` | IBM QRadar | AQL | yes | yes | as a `--` header |
      | `elastic` | Elastic Security | EQL | yes | yes | as a `//` header |
      | `wazuh` | Wazuh | XML | yes | yes | `<description>` |
      | `chronicle` | Google SecOps | YARA-L 2.0 | yes | yes | `meta:` |
      | `crowdstrike` | CrowdStrike Falcon | FQL | yes | yes | no — see below |
      
      SPL and FQL cannot carry a rule's triage header: Splunk keeps that in a
      `savedsearches.conf` stanza, and an FQL filter is a single string with no comment
      syntax. Rendering into either reports `ANNOTATIONS_NOT_TRANSFERABLE` rather than
      losing the title and severity quietly.
      
      ---
      
      ## Three verdicts
      
      ```
      matched        rows survived the pipeline
      no_match       nothing survived, and the engine is confident
      not_evaluated  nothing survived, and the engine cannot be confident
      ```
      
      `not_evaluated` is the whole point. A rule testing a field your sample does not
      contain has not failed to match — the question was never answered, and saying
      `no_match` would be a lie an analyst would act on.
      
      An unapplied index-time filter is the one caveat that does *not* block a
      confident negative, because removing rows cannot create a match — unless the rule
      contains an anti-join, which asks for rows with no counterpart. Those keep the
      strict verdict.
      
      ---
      
      ## Refusals
      
      A refusal is a feature. Each one carries a code, the stage it came from, and a
      sentence saying what would have gone wrong:
      
      ```
      SEQUENCE_NO_JOIN_KEY    this sequence has nothing to join the steps on, so any
                              first event would pair with any later one anywhere in
                              the estate
      
      WAZUH_RENDER_NO_SORT    Wazuh has no ordering. A rule whose meaning depends on
                              order has no Wazuh form, and writing it without the
                              ordering returns a different event
      
      SPL_GENERATING_TSTATS   `tstats` reads an accelerated summary, not events, so
                              there is nothing for a sample to be tested against.
                              Rewrite it as a `search` over an index
      ```
      
      The list is long on purpose. A tool that accepts everything and quietly
      approximates the hard parts is a tool that produces rules nobody can trust.
      
      ---
      
      ## Design principles
      
      **Every dispatch chain ends in a refusal.** Not a silent `else`, not a `pass`,
      not a `continue`. If a renderer meets a stage it cannot express, it says so by
      name. This is enforced by `tests/test_fidelity.py`, which sweeps a corpus of
      rules through every dialect pair and fails if any field name or literal value
      disappears without a diagnostic. That test exists because two renderers were
      cherry-picking stages out of the pipeline and dropping the rest — including
      thresholds.
      
      **Absent, null, empty and undecided are four different things.** A missing field
      is not an empty one. Sigma's `field: null` asks whether a field is present and
      null; KQL's `isnull()` has no such distinction because its schema is fixed. They
      lower to different predicates, deliberately.
      
      **Numbers are `Decimal` end to end.** A float threshold that compares unequal to
      itself is not a threshold.
      
      **A regex is only executed when the flavour can be honoured.** PCRE, PCRE2,
      OS-Regex and Java regex are refused rather than run through Python's `re` and
      reported as though they were the real thing. RE2 and POSIX ERE do execute,
      because on the portable subset they agree. Every pattern is screened for
      catastrophic backtracking first.
      
      **Nothing above the engine knows a vendor's syntax**, and nothing in the engine
      knows a vendor exists. That is what makes eight dialects possible without eight
      tools, and it is enforced by a test rather than by good intentions.
      
      ---
      
      ## Project structure
      
      ```
      RuleForge/
      ├── run.py                  the single entry point
      ├── engine/                 the vendor-neutral engine
      │   ├── cli.py              headless subcommands and the exit-code contract
      │   ├── ir.py               the rule model: 11 expression nodes, 13 stage nodes
      │   ├── values.py           ABSENT, UNDECIDED, Refusal, Duration, Capability
      │   ├── evaluate.py         three-valued expression evaluation, regex screening
      │   ├── pipeline.py         pipeline execution, verdicts, the stage trace
      │   ├── validate.py         structural lint and the ReDoS screen
      │   ├── codec.py            lossless tagged-JSON serialisation of a rule
      │   ├── store.py            append-only SQLite history with lineage
      │   ├── synthesize.py       log samples to a proposed rule
      │   └── dialects/           shared parser plus eight vendor languages
      │       ├── common.py       tokenizer and Pratt parser; a bug here is a bug
      │       │                   in all eight dialects at once
      │       ├── sigma.py  kql.py  splunk.py  qradar.py
      │       └── elastic.py  wazuh.py  chronicle.py  crowdstrike.py
      ├── web/                    the browser half
      │   ├── api.py              stdlib http.server: routing, limits, hardening
      │   ├── templates/          the Home + Studio interface
      │   └── static/             app.css, app.js
      ├── tests/                  1345 tests, standard-library unittest
      ├── corpus/                 403 real-shaped rules swept across every dialect pair
      ├── examples/               a rule pack with positive and negative fixtures
      ├── data/                   runtime only: saved rule history, never in git
      ├── pyproject.toml          packaging metadata
      └── README.md
      ```
      
      ---
      
      ## Testing
      
      ```bash
      python run.py verify
      ```
      
      That runs the suite and then the corpus sweep. The suite alone is:
      
      ```bash
      python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .
      ```
      
      `pytest` also works, but it is not the floor: a check that needs a dependency
      cannot run in the locked-down SOC this tool is built for.
      
      Three test modules are worth knowing about:
      
      **`tests/test_fidelity.py`** is a **sweep, not a set of cases.** It walks a corpus
      of rules through every dialect pair and asserts general properties: that no field
      name or literal value disappears without a diagnostic, and that every renderer
      emits text its own parser accepts. It exists because the suite was fully green
      while a renderer silently dropped thresholds — every test checked a conversion
      somebody had thought to check. A case tests what its author remembered; a sweep
      tests what nobody thought of. The second property, re-reading the output, found
      eight more defects the first one could not see, including a renderer emitting
      `count(1)` that the same module's parser rejects.
      
      **`tests/test_cli.py`** holds the BOM tests. A UTF-8 BOM silently renamed the
      first key of a rule, so a Sigma file saved by a Windows editor reported "this rule
      has no title" about a rule whose first line was the title. It was found because
      the CLI's own fixture was written with PowerShell, which adds one.
      
      **`tests/__init__.py`** holds `planned_dialect`, a synthetic registry entry. All
      eight dialects ship, so the planned-dialect refusal paths have no real dialect to
      point at — and pinning them to one that later shipped inverted them twice,
      silently, in this repository's history.
      
      ---
      
      ## Known limitations
      
      Stated because a tool that hides these is worse than one that does not have them:
      
      - **The sweeps are bounded by their corpus.** This is the honest limit, not a
        disclaimer: it is the mechanism by which two separate silent-widening bugs
        survived earlier rounds of "it's complete". A rule shape not in
        `tests/test_fidelity.py` is unexamined.
      
      - **An ABSENT field makes a comparison UNDECIDED, not False.** This is a
        deliberate open-world choice, and it has a cost worth knowing before you trust
        a verdict: `selection and not filter` — the commonest idiom in SigmaHQ —
        reports `not_evaluated` rather than matching when the filter's field is missing
        from the sample event, because `NOT UNDECIDED` is `UNDECIDED`. The real SIEM,
        compiling that rule against a fixed schema, would fire. So a sample event must
        carry the fields a rule's filters mention for the verdict to be decided. The
        engine says `not_evaluated` and names the absent field rather than reporting a
        confident non-match, which is the tradeoff being made: a loud "I don't know"
        instead of a quiet wrong answer. `RealRulesMatchTheRightEvents` pins it so it
        cannot change silently.
      
      - **The browser code has no behavioural tests.** Logic has been moved out of it
        where possible — synthesis, log parsing — but the form-to-IR binding and all
        rendering are unverified by the suite.
      
      - **Every dialect covers a subset of its language.** The refusals are honest, but
        `tstats`, `sample`, `eventstats`, multi-event YARA-L and a long list more are
        refused rather than supported. Known gaps found by running real vendor rules:
        Sigma's bare `keywords:` full-text search, multi-document Sigma (so
        `correlation` rules must be lowered one document at a time), SPL subsearches
        (`[ search ... ]`), and computed AQL `SELECT` expressions such as
        `LOGSOURCENAME(logsourceid) AS "Log Source"`. All four refuse by name rather
        than misreading.
      
      - **PCRE, PCRE2 and Java regex are modelled and rendered but never executed**, so
        a Sigma `|re` carrying PCRE or an AQL `MATCHES` is reported `not_evaluated`
        rather than guessed at. Wazuh OS-Regex and POSIX BRE are refused for a
        different reason — specific characters mean different things there — so a
        pattern containing none of those characters is executed exactly, which is what
        makes an ordinary Wazuh `<field>` rule locally testable.
      
      - **SPL and FQL cannot carry a rule's triage header**, and say so.
      
      ---
      
      ## Scope and security
      
      RuleForge is a workbench, not a service.
      
      - It binds to `127.0.0.1` by default and prints a warning if you point it
        anywhere routable.
      - It does not ship rules to a SIEM, and it has no deployment connector.
      - It does not pretend to know your data volume: a threshold it proposes is a
        number it chose, and it says so.
      - It reads and writes only local files, and stores history in a local SQLite
        database under `data/`.
      
      ---
      
      ## Requirements
      
      - **Python 3.10 or newer.** The floor is real: the model uses `slots=True`
        dataclasses, which 3.9 does not accept.
      - **Nothing else.** The engine, every dialect, the HTTP server and the entire
        test suite import only the standard library. There is no PyYAML, no Flask, no
        pytest requirement — the YAML reader, the HTTP server and the test harness are
        all written against the stdlib.
      
      That constraint is deliberate. It is what lets RuleForge run unmodified inside a
      locked-down SOC where `pip install` is not available.
      
      ---
      
      ## Contributing
      
      ```bash
      git clone https://github.com/EclipseManic/RuleForge.git
      cd RuleForge
      python run.py verify          # must be green before and after your change
      ```
      
      Guidelines:
      
      - **Keep the dependency count at zero.** Adding one is an architectural
        decision, not a convenience.
      - **Every new dialect feature needs a refusal for what it cannot express.** A
        silently dropped stage is a bug, even when the output looks right.
      - **Add a corpus rule** for any vendor syntax you start supporting, so the
        fidelity sweep covers it.
      - **Never weaken a test to get a green run.** If a test looks wrong, say so in
        the pull request.
      
      Issues and pull requests are welcome.
      
      ---
      
      ## License
      
      No license has been chosen for this project yet. Under the default, that means
      all rights are reserved. If you want to use, modify or redistribute RuleForge,
      please open an issue to discuss licensing first.
      
      
- path: run.py
  content: |
      """RuleForge -- one entry point for the whole tool.
      
      The pipeline every dialect plugs into:
      
          parse    native text  -> parsed structure
          lower    parsed       -> Rule          (the model in ir.py)
          render   Rule         -> native text
      
      Nothing above the engine is allowed to know a vendor's syntax, and nothing
      in the engine is allowed to know a vendor exists. That is what makes eight
      dialects possible without eight tools, and it is enforced by a test rather
      than by good intentions.
      
          python run.py                  open the browser workbench
          python run.py verify           the test suite, then the corpus sweep
          python run.py corpus --full    every corpus rule, with its message
          python run.py check sigma rule.yml
      
      This file is the only entry point. Every other tool in the suite starts with
      `python run.py`, and a tool that starts differently is a tool nobody remembers
      how to start. It also gives the two things that were only reachable by
      remembering a long command: the whole test suite, and the corpus sweep that
      the suite does not run.
      
      WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO
      
      * IT DOES NOT BIND 0.0.0.0 BY DEFAULT. This endpoint parses untrusted rule
        text and evaluates rules against untrusted samples, so it is loopback only
        and says so out loud if you override that.
      * IT DOES NOT PRINT A DIFFERENT PORT THAN THE ONE IT SERVES. If the preferred
        port is busy it names the one it actually bound.
      * IT DOES NOT NEED ANYTHING INSTALLED. `verify` runs unittest, not pytest,
        because a check that needs a dependency cannot run in the locked-down SOC
        this tool is built for. pytest works too; it is just not the floor.
      """
      
      from __future__ import annotations
      
      import argparse
      import socket
      import subprocess
      import sys
      import threading
      import time
      import webbrowser
      from pathlib import Path
      
      ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
      if str(ROOT) not in sys.path:
          # `python run.py` is meant to work from any working directory, and the
          # package it imports sits beside this file rather than on sys.path.
          sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))
      
      from web.api import build_server  # noqa: E402
      
      DEFAULT_HOST = "127.0.0.1"
      DEFAULT_PORT = 8765
      PORT_ATTEMPTS = 20
      
      HELP = """\
      RuleForge -- a detection rule workbench for enterprise SIEM rules.
      
          python run.py                  start the browser workbench (default)
          python run.py serve --port N   start it on a specific port
          python run.py verify           run the test suite, then the corpus sweep
          python run.py corpus [args]    sweep every dialect's corpus rules
      
      Every other command is the engine CLI, unchanged:
      
          python run.py dialects
          python run.py check     sigma    rule.yml
          python run.py explain   sigma    rule.yml
          python run.py convert   sigma sentinel rule.yml
          python run.py test      sigma    rule.yml events.jsonl
          python run.py propose   samples.jsonl --target sigma
      
      Exit codes: 0 the work succeeded, 1 a rule was refused or a conversion lost
      something, 2 the arguments were wrong.
      """
      
      
      def _port_is_free(host: str, port: int) -> bool:
          """True when nothing is already LISTENING on host:port.
      
          A connect probe rather than a bind, because a failed bind can mean
          permission or a stale socket as well as "in use", and only one of those
          is worth moving to the next port for.
          """
          with socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM) as probe:
              probe.settimeout(0.4)
              return probe.connect_ex((host, port)) != 0
      
      
      def _find_port(host: str, preferred: int) -> int:
          for offset in range(PORT_ATTEMPTS):
              candidate = preferred + offset
              if candidate > 65535:
                  break
              if _port_is_free(host, candidate):
                  return candidate
          raise SystemExit(
              f"Could not find a free port.\n"
              f"  Tried {preferred} to {preferred + PORT_ATTEMPTS - 1} on {host}.\n"
              f"  Something else may have them, or this account may not have\n"
              f"  permission to bind. Try:  python run.py serve --port 8080"
          )
      
      
      def _serve(argv: list[str]) -> int:
          parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
              prog="python run.py serve",
              description="Start the RuleForge browser workbench.",
          )
          parser.add_argument("--port", type=int, default=DEFAULT_PORT,
                              help=f"port to try first (default {DEFAULT_PORT})")
          parser.add_argument("--host", default=DEFAULT_HOST,
                              help=f"bind address (default {DEFAULT_HOST})")
          parser.add_argument("--no-browser", action="store_true",
                              help="do not open a browser")
          args = parser.parse_args(argv)
      
          if not 1 <= args.port <= 65535:
              parser.error(f"{args.port} is not a port")
      
          port = _find_port(args.host, args.port)
          try:
              server = build_server(args.host, port)
          except OSError as exc:
              print(
                  f"\nCould not start on port {port}: {exc}\n"
                  f"  Another program may have taken it between the check and the\n"
                  f"  start. Try again, or pass --port to choose one.\n",
                  file=sys.stderr,
              )
              return 1
      
          bound = server.server_address[1]
          url = f"http://{args.host}:{bound}/"
      
          # One write, flushed. Piped or redirected stdout is block-buffered, and a
          # banner that arrives only when the process exits is a banner that tells
          # nobody where the workbench went.
          lines = [
              "",
              "  RuleForge -- Detection Rule Workbench",
              f"  {url}",
          ]
          if bound != args.port:
              lines.append(f"  (port {args.port} was busy, so this is on {bound})")
          lines += [
              "",
              "  Eight dialects, one rule model, standard library only.",
              "  Ctrl+C to stop.",
              "",
          ]
          print("\n".join(lines), flush=True)
          if args.host not in ("127.0.0.1", "localhost", "::1"):
              print(
                  f"  WARNING: bound to {args.host}, which is not loopback. This\n"
                  f"  endpoint parses untrusted rule text and evaluates rules\n"
                  f"  against untrusted samples; it is a workbench, not a service.\n",
                  file=sys.stderr,
              )
      
          if not args.no_browser:
              threading.Thread(
                  target=lambda: (time.sleep(0.6), webbrowser.open(url)),
                  daemon=True,
              ).start()
      
          try:
              server.serve_forever()
          except KeyboardInterrupt:
              print("\n  Stopped.")
          finally:
              server.server_close()
          return 0
      
      
      def _run(command: list[str], label: str) -> int:
          """One check, with its own banner so a failure names what failed."""
          print(f"\n== {label} " + "=" * max(0, 58 - len(label)))
          code = subprocess.run(command, cwd=ROOT).returncode
          print(f"== {label}: {'ok' if code == 0 else 'FAILED'}")
          return code
      
      
      def _verify(_argv: list[str]) -> int:
          """Everything this repository can prove about itself, in one command.
      
          The suite first because it is fast and localised, then the corpus sweep
          because it is the only check that walks all 400-odd real-shaped rules
          through all eight dialects. A green suite alone has been misleading here
          before: it was fully green while a renderer dropped thresholds.
          """
          status = _run(
              [sys.executable, "-m", "unittest", "discover", "-s", "tests", "-t", "."],
              "test suite",
          )
          status = max(status, _run(
              [sys.executable, str(ROOT / "corpus" / "run_corpus.py")],
              "corpus sweep",
          ))
          print()
          print("  All checks passed." if status == 0
                else "  Something failed. See the banner above.")
          return status
      
      
      def _corpus(argv: list[str]) -> int:
          return subprocess.run(
              [sys.executable, str(ROOT / "corpus" / "run_corpus.py"), *argv],
              cwd=ROOT,
          ).returncode
      
      
      def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
          argv = list(sys.argv[1:] if argv is None else argv)
      
          if argv and argv[0] in ("-h", "--help", "help"):
              print(HELP)
              return 0
      
          if not argv or argv[0] == "serve":
              return _serve(argv[1:])
          if argv[0] == "verify":
              return _verify(argv[1:])
          if argv[0] == "corpus":
              return _corpus(argv[1:])
      
          # Anything else is the package's own CLI, handed over untouched so there
          # is one parser to learn rather than two that disagree.
          from engine.cli import main as engine_cli
      
          return engine_cli(argv)
      
      
      if __name__ == "__main__":
          raise SystemExit(main())
      
````

```
      async function doValidate() {
        try {
          const data = await call('POST', '/api/validate', {rule: readRule()});
          toast('This rule is structurally sound and no pattern in it would hang ' +
                'the engine that runs it.', 'good');
          renderMessages($('#diagnostics'), []);
          renderOutline($('#import-outline'), data.outline);
        } catch (err) {
          if (!err.handled) throw err;
        }
      }
      
      async function doRun() {
        const raw = $('#events').value.trim();
        if (!raw) { toast('paste at least one event to test against.', 'bad'); return; }
        /* The sample is sent as TEXT and parsed on the server. This used to parse
           here, with `parseLogs` and `coerce` -- which disagreed with the Python
           parser the From Log tab uses: JavaScript left `1.5` a string and `-` a
           string where Python produced a decimal and a null. The same pasted line
           meant different things in two tabs, and only one of the two parsers could
           be reached by a test. One parser now, and it is the tested one -- which
           also gives this box `kv` and `syslog` support it never had. */
        try {
          const result = await call('POST', '/api/evaluate', {
            rule: readRule(),
            text: raw,
            format: $('#events-format') ? $('#events-format').value
                  : (raw.startsWith('[') ? 'json' : 'jsonl'),
          });
          /* The stale flag is cleared only on a SUCCESSFUL run, so a verdict on
             screen always belongs to the rule on screen. */
          $('#evaluation').classList.remove('stale');
          renderEvaluation($('#evaluation'), result);
        } catch (err) {
          if (!err.handled) throw err;
          /* Cleared rather than left behind a refusal. A verdict under an error
             message is a verdict somebody will read. */
          $('#evaluation').classList.remove('stale');
          $('#evaluation').textContent = '';
        }
      }
      
      async function saveEvidence(targetSelector) {
        const target = $(targetSelector);
        const select = targetSelector === '#evaluation'
          ? $('#build-dataset') : $('#test-run-dataset');
        const datasetId = select ? Number(select.value) : 0;
        if (!datasetId) {
          toast('select a saved dataset before saving evidence.', 'bad');
          return;
        }
        try {
          const data = await call('POST', '/api/test-runs', {
            rule: readRule(),
            dataset_id: datasetId,
            expected_verdict: targetSelector === '#evaluation'
              ? $('#build-expected').value : $('#test-run-expected').value,
            purpose: targetSelector === '#evaluation'
              ? 'manual' : $('#test-run-purpose').value,
            note: targetSelector === '#evaluation'
              ? '' : $('#test-run-note').value,
            rule_entry_id: state.parentId,
          });
          state.selectedTestRunId = data.id;
          if (target) {
            target.classList.remove('stale');
            target.classList.remove('empty');
            renderEvaluation(target, data.result);
          }
          await loadTestRuns();
          toast('Evidence run ' + data.id + ' saved. The rule and dataset hashes are ' +
            'now linked in history.', data.matches_expected === false ? 'bad' : 'good');
        } catch (err) {
          if (!err.handled) throw err;
        }
      }
```

```
        'SecurityEvent',

        '| where ObjectName endswith "lsass.exe"',
        '| where AccessMask == "0x1410"',

      async function loadExample() {
        try {
          const data = await call('POST', '/api/lower',

          state.sourceText = EXAMPLE_RULE;
```

```
      /* ------------------------------------------------- condition editor */
      
      /** Render a condition subtree into `host`.
      
          `replace` is how a node swaps itself for a different one: a comparison that
          becomes an AND of two comparisons calls `replace(boolOp(...))`. Passing the
          setter down means no node needs to know its own address in the tree. */
      function renderCondition(host, expr, replace) {
        host.textContent = '';
        if (!expr) {
          const add = el('button', 'mini', '+ condition');
          add.onclick = () => { replace(newComparison()); };
          host.appendChild(add);
          return;
        }
      
        const kind = expr['@'];
      
        if (kind === 'BoolOp') {
          const wrap = el('div', 'cond');
          const head = el('div', 'cond-row');
          const label = el('span', 'cond-op-label', expr.op.v.toUpperCase());
          label.title = 'click to switch between AND and OR';
          label.style.cursor = 'pointer';
          label.onclick = () => {
            expr.op = T.str(expr.op.v === 'and' ? 'or' : 'and');
            renderCondition(host, expr, replace);
          };
          head.appendChild(label);
      
          const add = el('button', 'mini', '+');
          add.title = 'add another operand';
          add.onclick = () => {
            expr.operands.v.push(newComparison());
            renderCondition(host, expr, replace);
          };
          head.appendChild(add);
      
          const unwrap = el('button', 'icon', 'ungroup');
          unwrap.onclick = () => {
            // An empty BoolOp is the always-true predicate, which in a filter
            // matches every row -- so ungrouping collapses to the first operand
            // rather than leaving an empty group behind.
            replace(expr.operands.v.length ? expr.operands.v[0] : newComparison());
          };
          head.appendChild(unwrap);
          wrap.appendChild(head);
      
          expr.operands.v.forEach((operand, i) => {
            const slot = el('div');
            renderCondition(slot, operand, next => {
              if (next === null) {
                expr.operands.v.splice(i, 1);
                if (expr.operands.v.length === 0) { replace(newComparison()); return; }
                if (expr.operands.v.length === 1) { replace(expr.operands.v[0]); return; }
              } else {
                expr.operands.v[i] = next;
              }
              renderCondition(host, expr, replace);
            });
            wrap.appendChild(slot);
          });
          host.appendChild(wrap);
          return;
        }
      
        if (kind === 'Not') {
          const wrap = el('div', 'cond');
          const head = el('div', 'cond-row');
          head.appendChild(el('span', 'cond-neg', 'NOT'));
          const strip = el('button', 'icon', 'remove not');
          strip.onclick = () => { replace(expr.operand); };
          head.appendChild(strip);
          wrap.appendChild(head);
          const slot = el('div');
          renderCondition(slot, expr.operand, next => {
            if (next === null) { replace(null); return; }
            expr.operand = next;
            renderCondition(host, expr, replace);
          });
          wrap.appendChild(slot);
          host.appendChild(wrap);
          return;
        }
      
        if (kind === 'Comparison') {
          const row = el('div', 'cond-row');
      
          const scope = el('select', 'f-scope');
          scope.setAttribute('aria-label', 'Condition field scope');
          ['current', 'left', 'right'].forEach(s => {
            const option = el('option', null, s);
            option.value = s;
            if (expr.left['@'] === 'FieldRef' && expr.left.scope.v === s) {
              option.selected = true;
            }
            scope.appendChild(option);
          });
          scope.title = 'which row this field is read from. left and right are the ' +
                        'two sides of a join and mean nothing outside one.';
          scope.onchange = () => {
            expr.left = fieldRef(fieldRefText(expr.left), scope.value);
          };
          row.appendChild(scope);
      
          const name = el('input', 'f-name');
          name.type = 'text';
          name.setAttribute('aria-label', 'Condition field name');
          name.value = fieldRefText(expr.left);
          name.placeholder = 'win.eventdata.Image';
          name.onchange = () => {
            expr.left = fieldRef(name.value, scope.value);
          };
          row.appendChild(name);
      
          const op = el('select', 'f-op');
          op.setAttribute('aria-label', 'Condition operator');
          COMPARISON_OPS.forEach(o => {
            const option = el('option', null, o);
            option.value = o;
            if (expr.op.v === o) option.selected = true;
            op.appendChild(option);
          });
          op.onchange = () => { expr.op = T.str(op.value); };
          row.appendChild(op);
      
          const value = el('input', 'f-value');
          value.type = 'text';
          value.setAttribute('aria-label', 'Condition comparison value');
          value.placeholder = 'value';
          /* A REGEX right-hand side is shown as its pattern, and edited back into a
             Regex -- keeping its flavour and its case-insensitivity.
      
             It used to show an empty box: `literalToText` only understood a
             `Literal`, so a condition like `ObjectName endswith "lsass.exe"` --
             which this dialect folds into a case-folding regex -- appeared as the
             operator `matches` with NO value. The analyst could not see the
             pattern, and typing in that box replaced the Regex with a plain string,
             silently turning a case-insensitive suffix test into a case-sensitive
             exact match. The rendered pane showed the truth while the editor showed
      
      [read_files: showing lines 310-449 of 2308. Use code_search to locate the part you need and read a window around it, or call read_files again with offset=450 to continue.]
      
      function renderStages() {
        const host = $('#stages');
        host.textContent = '';
        const stages = state.rule.rule.pipeline.v;
      
        stages.forEach((stage, index) => {
          const kind = stage['@'];
          if (kind === 'Read') return;  /* edited in the left column */
      
          const card = el('div', 'stage' + (kind === 'Emit' ? ' terminal' : ''));
          const head = el('div', 'stage-head');
          head.appendChild(el('span', 'stage-kind', kind));
          head.appendChild(el('span', 'stage-id', stage.id.v));
          if (stage.capability && stage.capability.v === 'declared_only') {
            const badge = el('span', 'badge declared', 'appliance only');
            badge.title = 'modelled and rendered correctly, but only the vendor ' +
                          'engine can run it';
            head.appendChild(badge);
          }
```

# The whole tool in one sentence

> A **rule** is "if an event looks like *this*, shout". RuleForge lets you write that rule **once**, see it in **8 SIEM languages**, test it against **sample logs**, and keep a **receipt** of every version.

That's it. Everything else is a tab on the way to that.

# The map: what each tab is for

| Tab | In kid words | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| **Workbench** | Build the rule, see it in another language | You know what you want to match |
| **Import & Explain** | Paste someone else's rule, get plain English back | You found a rule online and don't trust it |
| **From Log** | Show it 3 log lines, it guesses a rule | You have logs but no idea what fields matter |
| **Datasets** | A **saved box of sample logs** | You want to reuse the same logs later |
| **Test Runs** | A **receipt**: "rule X got verdict Y on dataset Z" | You want proof for later |
| **History** | Every version you ever saved | "What did this rule look like before I broke it?" |

---

# Step 0 — Meet a finished rule (30 seconds)

1. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8765/`
2. Click the big **"Open a worked example"** button.

You land in the Workbench with a real rule filled in, and a sample log under *"Test against a sample"*.

3. Top-right there's a **Target** dropdown and next to it **Save version**. Change **Target** from `sentinel` to `splunk`, then `sigma`, then `qradar`.

Watch the **Rendered** pane on the right. **Same rule. Different language.** That's the whole product in one gesture.

4. Press the **Run** button in *"Test against a sample"*. You get `matched`. You just tested a detection without a SIEM.

---

# Step 1 — Import & Explain (paste a rule, read what it really says)

Click **Studio → Import & Explain**. Paste this into the big box:

```kql
// title: Encoded PowerShell launched from Word
// severity: high
SecurityEvent
| where ObjectName == "powershell.exe"
| where CommandLine contains "-enc"
| where ParentImage == "winword.exe"
```

Leave the dialect as `sentinel`. Click **"Analyze and load into builder"**.

**You should see** "What this rule says" on the right — in plain words, three conditions. And no red diagnostics, meaning nothing got lost in parsing.

This is your Exercise 1, expressed as a rule. Copy that KQL somewhere; you'll reuse it.

---

# Step 2 — Workbench (change the language, not the logic)

Click **Studio → Workbench**. The rule is now sitting in editable pieces:

- **Left column** — paperwork: `Rule id`, `Title`, `Severity`. Type `Encoded PowerShell from Word` into **Title**.
- **Middle column** — the actual logic. You'll see a `Read` card (where events come from) and **three Filter cards**, one per `where`, plus an `Emit` at the bottom.
- **Right column** — the language output, plus the test box.

Now the fun part. With the **Target** dropdown top-right, switch to `splunk`:

```
index=SecurityEvent
| where ObjectName == "powershell.exe"
| where match(CommandLine, "\-enc")
| where ParentImage == "winword.exe"
```

…and you'll get an **amber warning**: `ANNOTATIONS_NOT_TRANSFERABLE`. That is not an error. It means *"Splunk has nowhere to store a title and severity, so your logic survived but the alert name and severity did not."* The tool tells you what it couldn't carry instead of losing it silently. **Amber = read it. Red = it refused and will not guess.**

Each Filter card has a tiny `×` and arrows — that's how you delete or reorder a step. Inside a filter: a scope box (`current`), the field name, an operator, and the value. That's the grammar: **field · operator · value**.

---

# Step 3 — Test against a sample (the real one)

Still in Workbench. Scroll to **"Test against a sample"**, format **`one JSON object per line`**. Delete whatever is there and paste your Exercise 1 logs:

```jsonl
{"EventID":1,"ObjectName":"powershell.exe","CommandLine":"powershell.exe -enc SQBFAGgA","ParentImage":"winword.exe"}
{"EventID":1,"ObjectName":"powershell.exe","CommandLine":"powershell.exe -File C:\\Scripts\\backup.ps1","ParentImage":"winword.exe"}
{"EventID":1,"ObjectName":"cmd.exe","CommandLine":"cmd.exe /c powershell.exe -enc AAAA","ParentImage":"winword.exe"}
{"EventID":1,"ObjectName":"powershell.exe","CommandLine":"powershell.exe -enc BBBB","ParentImage":"explorer.exe"}
```

Press **Run**. Verdict: **`matched`**, **1 row kept**, and a stage-by-stage trace:

```
main_read     Read    0 → 4
main_where_0  Filter  4 → 3   dropped 1   ← cmd.exe isn't powershell.exe
main_where_1  Filter  3 → 2   dropped 1   ← no "-enc" in the -File one
main_where_2  Filter  2 → 1   dropped 1   ← parent is explorer.exe, not winword.exe
main_out      Emit    1 → 1
```

**Read the trace out loud.** Each condition is doing exactly one job, and you can see which event each step threw out. That's how you know a rule isn't accidentally broken — not by staring at it.

You'll also see a **caution**: `TIME_FIELD_NOT_FOUND`. Ignore it here — it only matters for rules that count over a time window, which this one doesn't.

# Step 6 — History (time travel)

1. Go back to **Workbench**, top-right, click **Save version**. Toast: *"Saved version 1. The next save will record itself as derived from it."*
2. Now **break the rule on purpose** — change one filter's value from `winword.exe` to `excel.exe`.
3. **Save version** again.
4. Open **Studio → History**.

You see two versions, marked `authored`, and the **Lineage** pane shows the second was derived from the first. That is the answer to *"what did this look like before I touched it, and why did I change it?"*

---

# The one concept that will make you feel stupid, then smart

There are **three** verdicts, not two:

- **`matched`** — a row survived.
- **`no_match`** — nothing survived, **and the tool is sure**.
- **`not_evaluated`** — nothing survived, and the tool **can't be sure**.

I tested this live: same rule, one good event plus one event that has **no `ParentImage` field at all**. Result: `not_evaluated`, `undecided: 1`.

Why isn't it "no match"? Because "the field isn't there" is not the same as "the field says explorer.exe". A missing field means *the question was never answered* — so it refuses to fake a confident answer. **If you ever see `not_evaluated`, add the missing field to your sample**, don't add a condition.

---

# From Log — and why it won't write your whole rule

Click **Studio → From Log**, paste these three lines, press **"Analyze samples and propose a rule"**:

```jsonl
{"EventID":1,"ObjectName":"powershell.exe","CommandLine":"powershell.exe -enc SQBFAGgA","ParentImage":"winword.exe"}
{"EventID":1,"ObjectName":"powershell.exe","CommandLine":"powershell.exe -File C:/Scripts/backup.ps1","ParentImage":"winword.exe"}
{"EventID":1,"ObjectName":"powershell.exe","CommandLine":"powershell.exe -enc BBBB","ParentImage":"explorer.exe"}
```

It reports:

| Field | Stable? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `EventID` | ✅ pinned | same in all 3 |
| `ObjectName` | ✅ pinned | same in all 3 |
| `CommandLine` | ❌ skipped | 3 different values |
| `ParentImage` | ❌ skipped | 2 different values |

Proposed rule: `EventID == 1 AND ObjectName == "powershell.exe"`.

**That's correct behaviour, and it's the important lesson.** A rule that pinned `CommandLine` would match exactly those 3 log lines and nothing else — the classic broken detection. Machine learning can't invent *"contains -enc"*; only you know that. So: **From Log gets you 80% of the boring part, you author the meaningful part.** That's why the proposed rule is labelled `synthesized` (a guess) and not `authored` (a decision).

---

# Gotchas that will bite you (learned the hard way, by me, minutes ago)

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `line 2 is not valid JSON: Invalid \escape` | Windows paths in JSON need **double** backslashes | `"C:\\Scripts\\backup.ps1"` — two characters, always |
| `not_evaluated` | your sample is missing a field a filter mentions | add the field to the event |
| Something is `#000000`-black in Datasets | that's what you saw earlier — a stale row | fixed; restart the server |
| Splunk/QRadar output has an amber warning | SPL/FQL can't hold title/severity | copy the title into `savedsearches.conf` yourself |
| Empty rule / "—" in Rendered | press **Render** after edits | or press **Validate** to lint it |
| Can't delete a dataset | there's no delete in the UI, by design (evidence is append-only) | remove the row from `data/history.sqlite3`, or ask me |

# CLI, for when you want this in CI

Same engine, no browser:

```bash
python run.py dialects                              # list the 8 languages
echo '<kql above>' | python run.py explain sentinel -   # what does it match
echo '<kql above>' | python run.py convert sentinel splunk -
python run.py test sentinel rule.kql events.jsonl   # exit 0 matched, 1 not
python run.py verify                                # full suite + corpus sweep
```

Exit code `1` on a lossy conversion is deliberate: a pipeline can't deploy a widened rule without noticing.

## What's actually on the Workbench screen

I counted the real markup in `index.html`:

| | count |
|---|---|

| …after a 3-condition rule (like your Exercise 1) | **~39** — every Filter card adds 6 more |
| Tabs across the top | **6**, all visible, all equal weight |

Thirty-nine live decisions, six headings, no numbering, no "start here". That's the root cause in one line: **the screen shows everything at once, so nothing looks like the next step.** Complexity isn't the number of features — it's the number of *visible choices with no ordering cue*. Your brain has to hold all 39 open at once because the layout never tells it which one to drop.

## The four reasons underneath that

**1. It shows you the engine, not your task.** The labels are the source code's vocabulary: `Read`, `Filter`, `Emit`, `stage id`, `scope: current`, `capability: evaluated`, `origin: authored`, `hash`, `not_evaluated`, `ANNOTATIONS_NOT_TRANSFERABLE`. Every one of those is a *real and honest* concept — but it's named by the person who wrote the engine, so you have to translate ~12 invented nouns before you can do anything. Someone who knows SIEM reads them instantly; someone learning reads them as noise, and noise is what "too much merged up" feels like.

**2. The tabs are organised by module, not by task.** *Workbench · Import & Explain · From Log · Datasets · Test Runs · History.* Not one of those is a verb you'd say out loud, and none is called "Start". So the natural first question — *what do I click first?* — has no answer anywhere on the screen. That's not your fault; it's the tab names.

**3. It opens in "you must already know" mode.** Every tab starts empty. The one thing that would make it click immediately — a complete rule that already runs, with real numbers — is hidden behind a button on the home page. Empty state + 39 controls + foreign nouns = learned helplessness, which is exactly the feeling you described.

**4. It was built to be *honest* before it was built to be *learnable*.** This is the deep one. The tool refuses to guess, keeps hashes, stores immutable evidence, warns when Splunk can't carry a title, and says `not_evaluated` instead of lying. All of that is genuinely good engineering — and every single safeguard adds one more thing on screen for a beginner to skip past. Correctness and first-run clarity pull in opposite directions here, and this tool spent its budget on the first. **It's not badly made. It's made for an expert's second week, not a beginner's first ten minutes.**

And that last sentence is also why it feels like "a wall": you're being handed a professional instrument's full control panel while still learning which end points at the target. A pilot doesn't learn on the full cockpit either.

## The one idea that would collapse most of it

If I could put one sentence on that screen, it'd be this:

> **A rule is a chain of sieves. Each Filter throws events away. Nothing else on this page matters until a sieve has thrown something away.**

Everything currently on that screen is a footnote to that sentence — and the tool already computes the good part for you (the trace you saw: `4 → 3 → 2 → 1`, each step dropping exactly one event). That trace is the whole tool. It's just buried under the paperwork, the language output, and the evidence form.

## What I'd change, smallest first

1. **A guided strip at the top of Workbench** that runs four steps and hides everything else: *what do you want to catch → here's the rule → here are your test logs → save the receipt.* One question visible at a time. Maybe 40 lines of JS and a CSS class — turning 39 controls into 4.
2. **Rename the tabs to verbs**: Build a rule · Check someone else's · Draft from logs · Sample logs · Test receipts · Versions.
3. **Retire the raw nouns** (`Read`, `stage id`, `scope`) from labels behind a "details" toggle — the concepts stay, the jargon goes.

None of those touch the engine, the tests, or the safety guarantees. They only change what the first screen *admits to*.

Want me to build #1 first? It's the smallest change that would take your "nothing is clear" to "oh, it's four steps", and I'd leave everything else exactly as it is.

I measured it, and "over-fabricated" is exactly the right word. Here's the evidence, then the plan.

## What's actually wrong (measured, not vibes)

| Metric in `index.html` today | Count |
|---|---|
| Hint paragraphs explaining the UI | **15** |
| Code comments of the form *"this was renamed because…"* | **22** |
| Stage types offered in one dropdown | **10** |
| Separate places that run a rule and show results | **3** |
| Controls visible on the Build screen for a 3-condition rule | **~39** |

Those first two numbers are the root cause, and they're not random. Look at the actual comments:

> *"Heading changed from 'Rule': this column is the rule's paperwork, not the rule."*
> *"These three had no explanation anywhere in the page… the only way to find out what they meant was to type something and see what happened."*
> *"The heading was 'Pipeline', which names the implementation rather than the thing."*

**The tool grew by adding an explanation every time something confused someone** — including you, eight times. Fifteen paragraphs and twenty-two renames later, the confusion hasn't been removed; it has been *documented in place*. That's what over-fabrication is here: the UI is a museum of every previous confusion, each one preserved with a placard. That's why reading it feels like homework and using it feels like guessing.

And the third number is worse than it looks: **three** different buttons can run your rule (`Run`, `Run and save evidence`, `Run and save evidence` in Test Runs). A first-timer cannot know which one is "the" one, so they pick wrong, get a different-looking result, and conclude they did it wrong. Nothing in the design disagrees with them.

## My plan: one guided front door, and hide the rest

Not a rewrite. The engine is good — 1345 tests, honest refusals, real hashes. All the value is there. The problem is 100% the first screen, so that's the only thing I'd touch.

**Step 1 — Add a 4-step Guided pane, and make it the landing page.**

Four screens, one question each, no more than 5 controls visible at a time:

1. **"What do you want to catch?"** — three choices: *start from a template* / *paste a rule I found* / *paste some logs*. Whichever you pick fills the rest, so you are never staring at an empty box. (This is the empty state that's killing you, killed.)
2. **"Here's what that means, in English"** — the rule as three plain rows: *ObjectName is powershell.exe* · *CommandLine contains -enc* · *ParentImage is winword.exe*. Editable inline. No `Read`, no `stage id`, no `scope`.
3. **"Test it"** — sample box pre-filled, one **Test** button, and the sieve trace `4 → 3 → 2 → 1` as the *headline*, not buried in a JSON blob.
4. **"Save the receipt"** — dataset + expected verdict + one button. Done.

Every one of those calls the API that already exists. **Zero engine changes, zero test changes.** It's one new pane (~120 lines of HTML), one new JS file (~200 lines) reusing `lower`/`render`/`evaluate`/`datasets`, and one CSS class to hide the other panes.

**Step 2 — Collapse the three things that are tripling the screen.**
- 10 stage types → show **Filter** only; the other 9 go behind *"+ advanced step"*.
- 8 paperwork fields → show **Title** only; the rest behind *"more fields"*.
- 15 hint paragraphs → delete them. If a field needs a paragraph, it needs a better label or to be hidden. **A hint paragraph is a failed label.**

**Step 3 — Rename the tabs to verbs** (5 minutes, removes the "where do I start" question): *Start here · Build a rule · Check someone else's · Draft from logs · Sample logs · Test receipts · Versions*.

**Step 4 — Kill the two duplicate evidence panels.** Keep exactly **one** button in the whole app that runs-and-saves. Three is how a beginner learns to distrust their own results.

`Risk: very low. The old Workbench stays reachable under an "Advanced" link, so nothing is lost and nothing can break.` Rough scale: Step 1 is the bulk of it, Steps 2–4 are small edits to the same file.

## What I would *not* do

- **Not** rewrite the UI from scratch. You'd throw away the one thing this tool does better than a real SIEM: telling you when it can't be sure.
- **Not** delete the 10 stage types or the 8 metadata fields. They're the reason a professional would use this. **Hide, don't delete** — an expert clicks "advanced" once and never notices.
- **Not** add a product tour. A tour is an apology for a bad screen; tours get clicked away in 3 seconds, exactly as you'd expect.
- **Not** write more docs. You already got a from-scratch walkthrough from me and it still feels heavy — that's proof the docs aren't the bottleneck, the first screen is.

## The one decision you have to make first

**Who is this tool for?**

- **If it's a portfolio / "look what I built" piece** → do all four steps. The 30-second demo *is* the product, and right now nobody can demo it without you narrating. That's the actual gap.
- **If it's for you, personally, on your own rules** → skip the UI work entirely. Use the CLI (`check` / `convert` / `test`) and the trace, and stop paying for a browser you don't need. The guided pane would be for visitors, not for you.

My honest read: you built something genuinely serious, and then kept patching the shopfront instead of building a door. **The plan is one door, four steps, everything else behind it.**

Tell me which of those two you are, and I'll start with Step 1 + 3 — the guided pane and the tab renames — since together they're what turns *"I have no idea"* into *"oh, it's four steps."*

```js
read.table  = T.str($('#read-table').value.trim() || 'events');
```

So **moving `#an-title` into its own tab needs zero JS changes.** Panes are hidden with a class, not removed, so the elements stay in the DOM and every function keeps finding them. What you're asking for is mostly a **markup re-layout**, not a rewrite — and it's verifiable: I can diff the set of element ids before and after and prove nothing was lost.

## The one trap to avoid

Thirteen flat tabs is not "easier" — it's a second wall. The mechanism that makes many tabs work is **grouping + a visible path + a persistent "which rule am I editing?" bar.** So the plan has three parts: the tab map, the shell that holds it together, and the rule that each surface owns exactly one job.

## The shell (what makes 13 tabs navigable)

1. **Grouped tab bar**, four groups separated visually: `AUTHOR · VERIFY · DERIVE · REFERENCE`.
2. **A step rail** across the AUTHOR tabs — `1 Details · 2 Source · 3 Conditions · 4 Preview · 5 Test · 6 Receipt` — with a **Next step →** button at the bottom of each. That gives the missing ordering cue *without hiding anything*: every tab is always visible, but there's an obvious walk through them.
3. **A persistent rule bar** at the top of every rule-related tab: `Editing: Encoded PowerShell from Word · enc-ps-001 · 3 conditions · ● unsaved · [Save version]`. This is the thing that stops "many tabs" from becoming "I lost my work".
4. **Ctrl+K** jump-to-anything over the 13 tabs + recent rules.

## The tab map — 13 surfaces, one job each

**AUTHOR — these tabs *change* the rule**

| Tab | Its one job | Owns exactly |
|---|---|---|
| **Start** | Pick where to begin | 4 templates, 5 recent versions, 3 doors (build / explain / draft), README quick-start |
| **1 Details** | Name the rule | rule id, title, description, severity, author, MITRE, references, false positives — full width, each with room to breathe |
| **2 Source** | Say where events come from | table, index-time selector, time field, + the "a sample can't reproduce a selector, so a test says so" note |
| **3 Conditions** | Build the filters | the Filter list only: one full-width row per condition (scope · field · operator · value · AND/OR · delete · duplicate · reorder), + Add condition |
| **4 Stage Library** | Every other step kind, properly | 9 cards — Aggregate, Correlation, Sequence, Distinct, Project, Derive, Sort, Limit, Expand — each with a **full form of its own** and an *Insert into rule* button, plus a worked example of what it renders to |
| **5 Preview** | See the other language | dialect picker with all 8 listed and a one-line description each, rendered output, diagnostics, Copy button, **Render** + **Validate** |

**VERIFY — these tabs *never* change the rule (read-only views of it)**

| Tab | Its one job | Owns exactly |
|---|---|---|
| **6 Test** | Does it catch what I mean? | sample box, 4 formats (JSONL / JSON array / key=value / syslog), one **Test** button, verdict headline, the sieve trace, per-condition drop reasons. **No save button. Ever.** |
| **7 Datasets** | Store sample logs | create form, list, detail pane with normalized events + hash + labels |
| **8 Receipts** | Evidence | dataset + expected verdict + "Run and save evidence" — **the only save-run button in the whole app** — then evidence detail and the recent-runs log |
| **9 Versions** | Time travel | version list with filters (`q`, origin, dialect), lineage graph, diff against parent |

**DERIVE — make a rule from something else**

| Tab | Its one job | Owns exactly |
|---|---|---|
| **10 Explain** | What does this pasted rule really say? | paste box + dialect, plain-English outline, diagnostics, *"load into Conditions"* |
| **11 Draft from Logs** | Guess a rule from samples | samples, options, field-stability table (pinned / skipped + why), proposed rule, *"load into Conditions"* |

**REFERENCE — where the explanations finally live**

| Tab | Its one job | Owns exactly |
|---|---|---|
| **12 Reference** | The vocabulary, in one place | verdict glossary (`matched` / `no_match` / `not_evaluated` + why undecided wins), the 8-dialect capability matrix (what transfers, what warns, what refuses), refusal codes, the "selector/time field aren't testable" facts |

## Why this fixes *your* three complaints specifically

- **"Tons of things under one tab"** → the Build screen's 6 headings and ~39 controls split into 6 tabs of 3–6 controls each, at full width instead of three cramped columns.
- **"Nothing is clear"** → every tab's name is its job, and the Reference tab means a term is explained *once, where you can go read it*, instead of 15 hint paragraphs scattered around. That's the trade I'm making with you: **the explanations don't disappear, they get a home and a single owner.**
- **"I don't know which button to press"** → only **5 Preview** renders, only **6 Test** tests, only **8 Receipts** saves. Right now three different buttons run a rule; that ambiguity dies by construction.

## Sequence and risk

1. **Shell first** — grouped tab bar, step rail, rule bar, `Ctrl+K`. Nothing else moves. Small.
2. **Split the Build pane** into tabs 1–6. Pure markup moves, ids unchanged, then I diff the id sets to prove nothing dropped. This is the bulk of it, and it's the *least* risky kind of change there is.
3. **Stage Library** — 9 dedicated forms replacing the 10-option dropdown.
4. **Reference tab**, then delete the 15 hints.
5. Re-home Explain / Draft / Datasets / Receipts / Versions into the new groups.

**Honest trade-off:** an end-to-end demo goes from "one long scroll" to "six hops". You gain clarity and a place for everything; you lose the at-a-glance single page. The step rail's **Next step →** is what buys that back, and for an expert tool that trade is correct — this is exactly how Sentinel and Splunk ES split rule → schedule → test → history into separate screens.

Estimated shape of the work: `index.html` roughly doubles (607 → ~1100 lines), `app.js` mostly untouched because ids survive, `app.css` needs a grouped-tab-bar + step-rail style. Nothing in `engine/` or `tests/` is touched, so all 1345 tests stay green throughout.

You've landed on the actual answer, so let me show you the evidence that says you're right — then the plan for rebuilding the whole thing, including the part you care about most: **when something breaks, finding it in seconds.**

## Why a whole-UI rebuild is justified (measured, not opinion)

I looked at how the front end is wired, and there's a specific defect — not a taste problem:

```js
// app.js:1134 — metadata comes from the DOM
function readRule() {
  rule.rule_id = T.str($('#rule-id').value.trim() || 'rule');
  an.title     = T.str($('#an-title').value);
  read.table   = T.str($('#read-table').value.trim() || 'events');
}

// app.js:577 — but the pipeline comes from the in-memory IR
function renderStages() {
  const stages = state.rule.rule.pipeline.v;   // ← not the DOM
```

**The same screen has two different sources of truth.** Ask "where is the title?" — the DOM input. Ask "where are the conditions?" — the IR object. That single decision means every bug starts with *"is it the input, or is it the IR?"* — and there is no single place to look. That is precisely why this tool is hard to use *and* hard to debug: **it's the same defect wearing two hats.**

On top of that: 4,031 lines of UI (607 HTML + 2,308 JS + 1,116 CSS), patronised by 22 *"this was renamed because…"* comments and 15 hint paragraphs. That's not a design, it's sediment. Another targeted patch would be layer #23 — and you're right that it wouldn't fix the feeling, because the feeling comes from the foundation.

## Why "rebuild everything" is the *safe* option here

Here's the fact that makes this not reckless:

- The entire UI talks to the engine through **12 JSON endpoints** (`/api/lower`, `render`, `validate`, `outline`, `evaluate`, `synthesize`, plus `history`, `datasets`, `test-runs` and their GETs). Nothing more.
- `engine/` has its own test suite (1,345 tests) and does not care what the UI looks like.
- Therefore **the front end is a replaceable layer.** Rewriting it cannot damage the detection logic — and I can prove parity by running the *old* and *new* UI against the *same* endpoints and comparing outputs.

That's the key difference from most "let's redesign it all" projects: your engine/UI boundary is already clean. The expensive, dangerous part of a rewrite — the logic — doesn't have to move.

## The plan, with your second requirement built in

You said: *"even if there will be any issue it would be very easy to find it out."* That's not a testing afterthought, it's an architecture choice. So the rebuild carries seven diagnostic instruments, from day one:

| Instrument | What it kills |
|---|---|
| **One state object, DOM is a projection** — `dispatch()` → `state` → `render()`. Inputs never own truth. | "Is it the input or the IR?" — there's one answer now: look at `state` |
| **URL as state** (`#/rule/enc-ps-001/conditions`) | Refresh loses work; bug reports become un-reproducible. Now a bug is a URL |
| **Autosave draft** to localStorage | Losing 20 minutes of typing to a stray refresh |
| **Problems panel** (compiler-style), pinned to the bottom | 6 different places showing errors today. Now: one list — `code · plain cause · [fix this →]` that jumps to the exact control |
| **Status bar** always visible: target dialect · rule hash · dataset hash · last verdict · server health | "Which version did I just test?" — answered without asking |
| **Health screen** — pings all 12 endpoints, runs one rule end-to-end, reports green/red per check | "Something's broken" → one click → the broken endpoint named |
| **State inspector** (`Ctrl+Shift+D`) — live state + last request/response | Guessing what the app thinks is true |

Every error code keeps its code (`ANNOTATIONS_NOT_TRANSFERABLE`, `TIME_FIELD_NOT_FOUND`, `STORE_DATASET_CORRUPT`…) and gains **one plain sentence + one jump-link**, defined once in a Reference screen. That replaces all 15 hint paragraphs — the explanations don't vanish, they get a single owner and become reachable from where they're needed.

## Screens (built from a spec, not from the old DOM)

Same 13 surfaces as before — nothing hidden, one job each:

**AUTHOR:** Start · 1 Details · 2 Source · 3 Conditions · 4 Stage Library · 5 Preview
**VERIFY:** 6 Test · 7 Datasets · 8 Receipts · 9 Versions
**DERIVE:** 10 Explain · 11 Draft from Logs
**REFERENCE:** 12 Reference · Health

Held together by: grouped tab rail, a **1→6 step rail** with *Next step →*, a persistent **rule bar** (*Editing: Encoded PowerShell from Word · 3 conditions · ● unsaved · Save*), and `Ctrl+K` jump-to-anything.

## Phases — each one ends with a working app

- **P0 — Spec.** One page: screens, states, error model, component inventory. You approve it *before* code. This is the anti-sediment step: renames get debated here, not in 22 code comments.
- **P1 — Design system.** Tokens (type/spacing/colour) + ~10 components replacing 1,116 lines of ad-hoc CSS. Plus a **UI smoke harness** (endpoint ping + screen-renders assertions) so the new UI has a regression net from the start.
- **P2 — The shell.** Router, state store, rule bar, step rail, problems panel, status bar, toasts. Old UI still served at `/classic`.
- **P3 — The daily four:** Details, Source, Conditions, Preview. By the end of this, you can build and read a rule end-to-end without ever seeing the old page.
- **P4 — Test, Datasets, Receipts, Versions** (the evidence chain).
- **P5 — Start, Explain, Draft, Stage Library, Reference, Health.**
- **P6 — Parity check, then delete `/classic`.**

**What does not change:** `engine/`, the 12 endpoints, all 1,345 tests, and every honesty feature (`not_evaluated`, refusals, hashes, transfer warnings). They get *more* prominent, not less — the new UI has dedicated room for them instead of squeezing them into hint text.

**Honest cost:** this is the biggest thing we've discussed — roughly 4–5k lines of front-end rewritten, and there's no UI test suite today, which is why P1 adds one first. It will take several sessions, but each phase leaves you with something better than today, and `/classic` means you're never stranded.

**My defaults unless you say otherwise:** keep the current dark visual language (don't fix what isn't broken, and it keeps the diff reviewable), plain HTML/CSS/JS with no build step and no new dependencies — the same "standard library only" discipline the engine already keeps.

Say **go**, and I'll write P0 first: the spec page — screen by screen, control by control, with the error model — for you to approve or redline before a single line of UI code moves.
